coherence.reason: One claim, one question: is a three-way nuclear build-up under way, judged by the bodies that count warheads.

surprise:new-nuclear-arms-race-beginning.question: Is a new nuclear arms race really starting between the US, Russia and China?
surprise:new-nuclear-arms-race-beginning.title: Is a New Nuclear Arms Race Already Here?
alternates: The US, Russia and China: is the nuclear build-up real?
What the warhead counters say about a new nuclear arms race
surprise:new-nuclear-arms-race-beginning.whyWatch: The people who count warheads now call it an arms race, but their own numbers show only one of the three is growing its stockpile today; the gap between the label and the count is the story.
surprise:new-nuclear-arms-race-beginning.tension: SIPRI and the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists say arms-race dynamics are back and the post-Cold War fall in warheads is set to reverse, yet US and Russian stockpiles held steady in 2025 and the expansion so far is China's.
surprise:new-nuclear-arms-race-beginning.evidenceNeeded: Year-on-year warhead and deployment counts for the US and Russia after New START expired, showing whether the forecast rise has begun.
surprise:new-nuclear-arms-race-beginning.premise: Two expert bodies judge it an arms race: the Bulletin calls major-power competition 'a full-blown arms race', and SIPRI says the decades-long decline in warhead numbers is likely to reverse as dismantlement slows and new deployments accelerate. The limits matter. The growth in warhead numbers so far is China's (the DoD expects over 1,000 by 2030); for the US and Russia the evidence is modernization of delivery systems and a forecast rise, not yet bigger stockpiles. US intelligence describes the same modernizing and expanding forces without calling it an arms race, part of the Bulletin's case is about missile defence and space rather than warheads, and forecasters split: superforecasters expected global warhead numbers to rise, nuclear experts expected a fall.

arc.hook: With New START gone, is a three-way nuclear arms race starting?
arc.conflict: The watchdogs say yes; the stockpile counts for the US and Russia have not moved yet.
arc.evidence: SIPRI's reversal forecast and the Bulletin's 'full-blown arms race' judgment, against China's measured growth, US and Russian modernization, the ODNI's more cautious description and the split forecasts.
arc.resolution: The competition is real and building, with China growing now and the US and Russia modernizing; calling it a race in numbers on all three sides is a forecast, not yet a measurement.
arc.takeaway: An arms race in the making: judged by experts, measured so far mainly in China, and expected rather than observed for the US and Russia.

coherence.reason: Pruned from a list of eight unrelated claims to the two that answer one question: could the Iran war become a world war, which turns on whether Russia and China would fight for Iran.

decision:most-discussed-claims.question: Could a war with Iran turn into World War 3?
decision:most-discussed-claims.title: Could a War With Iran Become World War 3?
alternates: Iran, Russia and China: how close did the 2026 war come to a world war?
Would Russia and China fight for Iran?
decision:most-discussed-claims.whyWatch: The fear that an Iran war drags in Russia and China was tested in 2026: the war came to the brink of a wider regional war, and what Moscow and Beijing actually did is on the record.
decision:most-discussed-claims.tension: Commentators warned an attack on Iran could spark a world war; in the 2026 war the fighting stayed regional and Russia and China backed Iran with UN vetoes, not forces.
decision:most-discussed-claims.evidenceNeeded: Evidence on whether any great power beyond the US entered or prepared to enter the fighting, and assessments of Russian and Chinese willingness to defend Iran militarily in a future war.
decision:most-discussed-claims.premise: Two claims decide it. Would the war widen into a world war? The evidence supports regional, not world, escalation: the Doha Institute says forty days of fighting brought the region to the brink of a wider war and an energy crisis before a ceasefire, and PRIO says the Middle East escalation raises the risk of a large multi-country regional conflict; no study shows a path to a world war. Would Russia and China fight for Iran? In 2026 they did not: they vetoed a Security Council resolution on Hormuz and stayed out of the fighting. Estonian intelligence (EFIS) says Moscow tends to forget its allies in times of need, and the Pentagon judges Beijing reluctant to deepen its modest defence ties with Iran. The limits: that is one war and two separate judgments, one about Russia and one about China, not a guarantee for every future war; and no study puts a probability on a world war starting from Iran.

arc.hook: When the US and Israel went to war with Iran, people asked whether this was the start of World War 3.
arc.conflict: A world war needs great powers to join; the warnings assumed Russia and China would.
arc.evidence: The 2026 war reached the brink of a wider regional war, but Russia and China acted only at the UN; EFIS on Russia and the DoD on China explain why; PRIO frames the risk as regional.
arc.resolution: The evidence shows a real risk of a wider Middle East war and no sign of a world war: in 2026 Russia and China did not fight for Iran. That is the record of one war and analysts' judgments, not proof they never would.
arc.takeaway: Watch whether outside great powers commit forces; without that, an Iran war is a regional war, however dangerous.

conflict:china-headed-war.research: The question is a forecast of an event that has not happened, so no study can decide it. Every source is a forecast or a reading of history: Metaculus (wrong, 0.4: 8.7% before 2035), the FRI expert panel (0.35), Eurasia Group (0.3), DDIS (partly, 0.35: both sides preparing for a confrontation neither wants), the Atlantic Council strategist survey (partly, 0.25) and Hanania on the Thucydides-trap base rate (0.3); further expert surveys and superforecaster panels (CFR Preventive Priorities, the 2021 UnHerd superforecaster panel on Taiwan) are the same kind of evidence and would not reach 0.5. It unblocks only when there is an outcome to check, or if the story is reframed around why forecasters and strategists disagree (a method comparison of forecasting tournaments against expert surveys).

coherence.reason: One claim, one question: is there a Russia-China military alliance, judged by intelligence assessments of the relationship.

surprise:russia-china-have-formed-milita.question: Have Russia and China really formed a military alliance?
surprise:russia-china-have-formed-milita.title: Are Russia and China Military Allies?
alternates: Russia and China: close partners, but are they allies?
What intelligence agencies say about a Russia-China alliance
surprise:russia-china-have-formed-milita.whyWatch: The two powers drill together, fly joint bomber patrols and share weapons research, yet three intelligence services judge there is no alliance; the gap between close cooperation and a defence pact is what decides whether one would fight for the other.
surprise:russia-china-have-formed-milita.tension: Joint exercises, bomber patrols near Alaska and intensifying military research ties look like an alliance, but the Pentagon says Beijing and Moscow remain unwilling to give each other mutual security guarantees.
surprise:russia-china-have-formed-milita.evidenceNeeded: A treaty text or official assessment showing a mutual-defence commitment between Russia and China, or an independent study that confirms there is none.
surprise:russia-china-have-formed-milita.premise: The evidence does not support a formal military alliance. The Pentagon's 2025 China report says that despite growing ties Beijing and Moscow remain unwilling to establish a formal defence alliance with mutual security guarantees, still distrust each other, and that China has stopped short of giving Russia lethal aid for its war in Ukraine. US intelligence (ODNI 2026) calls cooperation among China, Russia, Iran and North Korea limited and primarily bilateral and says 'adversary alignment' overstates it. The limits matter: the cooperation is real and growing. China gives Russia diplomatic, defence-industrial and economic support, the two hold combined exercises and patrols, and Estonian intelligence (EFIS 2026) reports that joint military research has intensified markedly, while judging a formal alliance unlikely only in the near future. So the finding is about the absence of a defence pact today, not about how close the partnership is or what it could become.

arc.hook: Russia and China drill together and fly joint bomber patrols: have they formed a military alliance?
arc.conflict: The cooperation looks like an alliance, but an alliance means a promise to fight for each other.
arc.evidence: The DoD 2025 report: no formal defence alliance, no mutual security guarantees, mutual distrust, no Chinese lethal aid to Russia; ODNI 2026: limited, primarily bilateral cooperation; EFIS 2026: joint exercises and research ties growing, a formal alliance unlikely in the near future.
arc.resolution: They are close strategic partners with deepening military cooperation, but on these assessments there is no mutual-defence commitment.
arc.takeaway: Partners, not allies, for now: watch for a defence guarantee, not another joint exercise.

conflict:world-war-has-already-started.research: Whether a world war has started is a question of definition, not of measurement, and every source already in the corpus agrees it has not by the usual test (direct, sustained war among the major powers at global scale): UCDP 2025 (wrong, 0.4: eight interstate conflicts, all regional, no great-power dyad) and the two Metaculus resolution criteria (0.35, 0.3: 10 million dead and 30% of world GDP involved). The strongest further data in the corpus (PRIO Conflict Trends: 245,000 battle deaths in 2025, below 2021 and 1994; ODNI 2026: "even if the great powers refrain from conflict") measure the same thing and would not reach 0.5, and the web offers only commentary (Trenin, McMaster, IPS) on the "piecemeal" or hybrid-war reading, which no dataset tests. It unblocks if the story is reframed around the definition (what counts as a world war and why the hybrid-war framing escapes the conflict datasets), or once there is a direct great-power war to count.

coherence.reason: One claim, one question: is Russia paying North Korea in military technology, and for what.

surprise:russia-giving-north-korea-milit.question: Is Russia really giving North Korea military technology in return for its help?
surprise:russia-giving-north-korea-milit.title: What Is Russia Giving North Korea?
alternates: Russia, North Korea and the price of help in Ukraine
What US intelligence says North Korea gets from Russia
surprise:russia-giving-north-korea-milit.whyWatch: The usual story is shells for know-how, long told without public proof; eleven governments now document what goes each way, and the answer is narrower and more specific than the rumours.
surprise:russia-giving-north-korea-milit.tension: Officials have long hinted at Russian help with satellites and nuclear know-how without public proof; the documented record names air defence systems going to North Korea in exchange for its artillery, missiles and troops, and little beyond that.
surprise:russia-giving-north-korea-milit.evidenceNeeded: An official or independent assessment that itemises Russian technology transfers to North Korea beyond air defence systems, with their scale.
surprise:russia-giving-north-korea-milit.premise: The evidence supports the claim in a specific form. The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a reporting body of eleven governments including the US, Japan and South Korea, reports (2025) that in 2024 North Korea shipped artillery, ballistic missiles and combat vehicles to Russia for its war against Ukraine while air defence systems went from Russia to North Korea, and that in return for its military support North Korea gained resources to develop its ballistic missile programmes and experience in modern warfare. US intelligence (ODNI 2026) adds that North Korean troops are gaining military technology from Russia for fighting against Ukraine. The limits matter. The documented transfer named is air defence systems; the summary does not itemise other technology or its scale. The price includes troops, not only arms: over 11,000 North Korean soldiers have been deployed. And the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (2026) expects Russian help to North Korea's nuclear and missile programmes to expand, but states that as likely, not documented. So Russia is paying North Korea partly in military hardware and know-how, for arms and soldiers together, and help with nuclear weapons remains a forecast.

arc.hook: North Korea sends Russia shells, missiles and soldiers for its war in Ukraine: what does it get back?
arc.conflict: The common account is shells for know-how, but the details have stayed unverified.
arc.evidence: MSMT 2025: North Korean artillery, ballistic missiles and combat vehicles to Russia, air defence systems from Russia to North Korea, and resources for North Korea's missile programmes in return for its military support; ODNI 2026: North Korean troops gain military technology from Russia for fighting against Ukraine; Bulletin 2026: Russian help to the nuclear and missile programmes will likely expand, stated as likely, not documented.
arc.resolution: Yes: military hardware and know-how are flowing to North Korea, paid for by arms and troops together; the documented item is air defence, and nuclear help is still a forecast.
arc.takeaway: Russia is paying in military technology; how much, and whether nuclear help follows, is not yet public.

coherence.reason: One claim, one question: who is ahead in the war in Ukraine in 2026, and what 'winning' amounts to.

surprise:russia-winning-war-ukraine-2026.question: Is Russia actually winning the war in Ukraine?
surprise:russia-winning-war-ukraine-2026.title: Is Russia Winning in Ukraine?
alternates: Who is ahead in Ukraine, according to the intelligence reports
Russia has the upper hand in Ukraine: but is that winning?
surprise:russia-winning-war-ukraine-2026.whyWatch: Headlines swing between 'Russia is winning' and 'Russia is stuck'; four intelligence and risk assessments from 2025-2026 agree on who has the edge and disagree with both headlines on what that edge is worth.
surprise:russia-winning-war-ukraine-2026.tension: US intelligence says Russia has kept the upper hand and expects to prevail; Danish intelligence, Eurasia Group and the Munich Security Report say the same edge buys slow gains, no breakthrough, and no victory in sight.
surprise:russia-winning-war-ukraine-2026.evidenceNeeded: An independent battlefield assessment for 2026 (territory changed hands, force and production balance) that says whether Russia's edge is turning into a decisive advantage.
surprise:russia-winning-war-ukraine-2026.premise: The evidence supports the claim only in a narrow form. US intelligence (ODNI, March 2026) says that during the past year Russia has maintained the upper hand in its war against Ukraine, that its forces continue to gain ground, and that Moscow almost certainly remains confident it will prevail on the battlefield; it also says US peace efforts could change this dynamic. Danish Defence Intelligence (2025) agrees Russia is gaining ground and is better positioned for a war of attrition, through recruitment and greater military production, but says it remains far from a military victory: Ukraine's resistance has prevented large-scale territorial gains, Russia had captured only around 1% of Ukraine's total territory by 2025, and neither side is likely to make significant battlefield advances in 2026, though the risk of sudden local breakthroughs grows as Ukrainian forces are worn down. Eurasia Group (January 2026) expects the fighting to grind on with no immediate breakthrough for either side, while Ukraine's position deteriorates. The Munich Security Report (February 2026) says only that Russia is seemingly regaining tactical initiative along parts of the front. So Russia holds the advantage and is gaining ground slowly; none of these assessments says it is close to winning, and the US view that Moscow expects to prevail is Moscow's confidence as the analysts read it, not a forecast of victory.

arc.hook: Is Russia winning the war in Ukraine, or stuck in it?
arc.conflict: US intelligence says Russia has the upper hand and expects to prevail; other assessments say no one is about to break through.
arc.evidence: ODNI 2026: Russia has maintained the upper hand over the past year and is confident it will prevail; DDIS 2025: gaining ground and better placed for attrition, but far from victory, about 1% of Ukraine's territory taken by 2025, no significant advances expected for either side in 2026; Eurasia Group 2026: no immediate breakthrough, Ukraine's position deteriorating; Munich Security Report 2026: Russia seemingly regaining tactical initiative along parts of the front.
arc.resolution: Russia is ahead, not winning outright: it holds the initiative and the attrition advantage, gains ground slowly, and no assessment expects a decisive breakthrough in 2026, though Ukraine is being worn down.
arc.takeaway: Winning here means a slow edge in a war of attrition, not a victory in sight; whether that edge turns decisive is the open question.
